notes.detailedSummary: Constructs the specified proper smooth strict analytic surface over C((s)), excludes separated finite-type algebraic-space algebraizations using disc/circle Picard, annulus filling, Laurent multiplier recurrence and analytic regularity, and fixes the degenerate positive datum with raw mass two. Proves all-point separation and vector-lattice density without global strict positivity. Deeper named analytic foundations remain conventional, not newly recursively audited.

# The analytic carrier, positivity datum, and separating tests

This is an independent proof draft relative to the conventional published foundations stated below. No supplied note or positive verdict is a premise. Put $K=\mathbf C((s))$, $|s|=e^{-1/8}$, $t=s^8$, $Y=(\mathbf G_m^2)^{\rm an}$ and $\Lambda=\langle(t,2),(3,t)\rangle$. On $Y$ let $x_i=-\log|z_i|$. Then $\Lambda$ translates $x$ by $\mathbf Z^2$. Let $X=Y/\Lambda$.

The following analytic foundations are retained. Conrad--Temkin, Non-archimedean analytification of algebraic spaces, author paper at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/analgpaper.pdf, Lemma 4.2.3: an etale equivalence relation has an analytic quotient if its restrictions to an ordinary open cover do; the resulting local quotients are open subspaces covering the quotient. Lemma 4.2.4: pullback is an equivalence between coherent G-sheaves and coherent descent data for a flat quasi-finite analytic surjection. Its proof reduces locally to finite faithfully flat affinoid algebras, where completed tensor products are ordinary ones. Closed immersions descend by their coherent ideals. Theorem 2.3.1 reflects separatedness and smoothness under analytification, and properness for finite-type maps; Example 2.3.2 compares algebraic and analytic stalks at closed points. The applied statements and complete immediate arguments were read in the retained primary extracts. Deeper Berkovich descent is a conventional source foundation.

Inverse images of tropical rectangles of coordinate widths less than one have disjoint nonidentity translates. They furnish ordinary open quotient charts. On bounded tropical ranges the relation is a finite union of disjoint closed deck graphs. A compact fundamental polyannulus $x^{-1}([0,1]^2)$ surjects onto $X$. Choose a finite cover of this square by injective charts. Their disjoint union maps to $X$ by a flat quasi-finite surjection, with finite fibres; its product has the same properties. The relation ideals on this cover have the deck cocycle, so coherent descent proves that the quotient diagonal is closed. This does not apply quasi-finite descent to the infinite-sheeted map $Y\to X$. Rectangles with endpoints in $(1/8)\mathbf Z$ and nested widths below one give strict affinoid neighbourhoods. Thus $X$ is compact Hausdorff, separated, good, strict, smooth, pure two-dimensional, boundaryless and proper. Connectedness follows from the connected nested Laurent polyannuli covering $Y$ and surjectivity of $Y\to X$.

Here is an independent nonalgebraization argument. Gruson, Fibres vectoriels sur un polydisque ultrametrique (1968), IV.5 Theorem 1, applies to finite completed tensor products of disc algebras with radii in the divisible valuation group and unit-circle algebras. It gives $SK^0(H)=0$ (and $SK^1(H)=0$, unused here). A rank-one projective module has the class of $H$; stable equality followed by determinants trivializes it. Only disc/circle factors are inputs to this theorem. Wide annuli are handled separately: a line bundle on $A(r,R)\times Z$ can be trivialized on $C(r)\times Z$, then glued to the trivial bundle on $D(r)\times Z$. The finite rational cover $D(r)\cup A(r,R)=D(R)$ has intersection $C(r)$. Induction on the number of wide factors trivializes the resulting line bundle on $D(R)\times Z$ and hence the original one. This uses Tate--Kiehl coherent gluing, in Van der Put, Rigid analytic spaces (1975--76), 2.14--2.16.3: coherence is local on finite affinoid covers, coherent sheaves on an affinoid are finite modules and have vanishing higher cohomology, with the indicated descent equalizer. The complete relevant text and the J7-09 diagram were read, including its explicit appeal to Kiehl. Consequently every $P_m=\{|s|^m\le |z_i|\le |s|^{-m}\}$ has Picard group zero.

We also need compatibility on the noncompact torus, not merely this finite result. If $b=\sum b_\beta z^\beta$ is a unit on $P_m$, its Gauss log norm is convex; its inverse has the opposite convex norm. The common norm is therefore affine. A monomial maximizing it at an interior point agrees with this affine norm throughout the tropical box. Writing that exponent as $\alpha$ gives
\[
 |b_\beta/b_\alpha|e^{(m/8)|\beta-\alpha|_1}\le1.
\]
Thus $b=b_\alpha z^\alpha(1+g)$, with zero constant coefficient and $\|g\|_{P_j}\le |s|^{m-j}$ for $j<m$. A global unit on $Y$ is a scalar monomial: any different exponent would dominate along some tropical ray. Normalize successive trivializing frames by scalar monomials, so $e_{m+1}=(1+g_m)e_m$ on $P_m$. On each fixed $P_j$ the products $p_j=\prod_{m=j}^{\infty}(1+g_m)$ converge to units; the first finitely many factors are already units and the remaining factors and inverse tails converge by the displayed bound. The frames $e_jp_j$ agree on overlaps. They glue on the interior exhaustion, proving $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)=0$.

An equivariant line bundle frame then has scalar-monomial multipliers $c_i z^{h_i}$. Write $h_1=(A,B)$, $h_2=(C,D)$. Commutativity gives $t^C2^D=3^At^B$, hence $C=B$, $A=D=0$. Thus $h_1=(0,k)$ and $h_2=(k,0)$. For $k\ne0$, take $\lambda=\lambda_1\lambda_2^{\operatorname{sign}k}$ and $h=(k\operatorname{sign}k,k)$. Then $Q=v(\lambda^h)=2|k|>0$. Any nonzero analytic section satisfying $f(\lambda z)=cz^h f(z)$ has Laurent coefficients
\[
 a_{m+jh}=a_m c^j\lambda^{-jm-hj(j+1)/2}.
\]
Their valuations have leading term $-Qj^2/2$, contradicting Laurent convergence on the unit polyannulus. For $k=0$, two nonzero coefficient exponents must have identical pairings with both period valuations and hence coincide. Every nonzero equivariant section is a single nowhere-vanishing monomial, and two sections with the same multipliers are proportional.

For a meromorphic fraction $F=g/h$ on the smooth torus, its pole ideal $J=\{b:bF\in\mathcal O\}$ is the coherent kernel of multiplication by $g$ into $\mathcal O/(h)$. In regular local rings cancellation makes this ideal principal of rank one. Stacks Tag 0AG0 says a regular local ring is a UFD; its complete induction proof was read. Flat analytic restrictions commute with this kernel and glue the ideal. The exact regularity inputs are Ducros, Families of Berkovich spaces, 2.1.3(2),(5): affinoid-domain and analytic-local restriction maps are regular; and 2.1.4: for a scheme locally of finite type over an affinoid algebra the algebraic-to-analytic local map is regular. These are published foundations, with their cited deeper Ducros/Berkovich proofs disclosed rather than freshly reconstructed. A global frame of $J$ on $Y$ produces holomorphic $f_0$ and $f_1=Ff_0$ with the same deck multipliers. The preceding recurrence makes $F$ constant. Therefore $\Gamma(X,\mathcal M_X)=K$.

If $X=Z^{\rm an}$ for a separated finite-type $K$-algebraic space, the reflection theorem makes $Z$ smooth and proper of dimension two. It is connected, hence integral: regularity separates its finitely many irreducible components. Stacks Tags 086U, 0BB1, 0EN6, 0ENA and 0END supply a dense scheme locus and $\Gamma(Z,\mathcal K_Z)=K(Z)$, of transcendence degree two. Their precise hypotheses are: decency for the dense scheme locus; finitely many irreducible components on quasi-compact etale scheme charts; all weak associates of codimension zero; and generic points represented by field monomorphisms for 0ENA. Separated finite-type smooth $Z$ satisfies these conditions. The exact statements and immediate proofs were read. Regular algebraic-to-analytic local maps preserve nonzerodivisors, so local fractions analytify and descend. A closed point in a nonempty scheme open avoiding numerator and denominator zeros detects a nonzero rational function. Thus $K(Z)$ injects into $\Gamma(X,\mathcal M_X)=K$, a contradiction. This excludes separated finite-type algebraic-space algebraizations at the specified base field. No assertion after every field extension is made.

Put $\rho=|x|^2/2$ and $\theta=DD\rho$, where $DD=d'd''$. Deck changes of $\rho$ are smooth affine functions, so $\theta$ descends as an ordinary smooth positive closed form with local smooth psh potentials. The ordinary identity-torus integration convention has saturated lattice $\mathbf Z^2$, degree one, and measure $2\det(\operatorname{Hess}F)\,dx$ for a convex smooth weight $F$, supported on its Gauss section. This is the conventional CLD calibrated integration rule, with the factor $2!=2$ retained. Applied to $\rho$ and the unit fundamental square it gives $\theta^2=2i_*dx$ and raw mass $M=2$.

Let $\mathscr P$ be the minimal continuous psh sheaf of CLD Definition 8.1.7, closed under local uniform limits, and let $\mathcal C=\{u\in C(X):\rho+u\in\mathscr P\text{ locally}\}$. Its convex/max closure follows independently as follows: convex combinations of smooth psh weights are psh, and their smooth convex soft maxima converge uniformly to their maximum. Fixing one smooth weight, the other weights for which either operation belongs to $\mathscr P$ form a sheaf closed under uniform limits and containing the smooth weights. Minimality gives every weight; fix such a weight and repeat the argument in the other slot. Thus both operations preserve $\mathscr P$ and, after adding the common local $\rho$, preserve $\mathcal C$. Constants are included. This class separates every pair of analytic points. Different tropical classes are separated by a small smooth periodic function $\varepsilon f(x)$ with $I+\varepsilon\operatorname{Hess}f\ge0$. For points in one tropical fibre, lift their common tropical coordinate to $a$ and take a chart $|x_i-a_i|<r<1/2$. Distinct seminorms differ on a Laurent polynomial $P$. Label them so $|P(p)|>|P(q)|$, and set $b=\log|P(p)|$. On the closed polyannulus let $L$ bound $\log|P|$ from above. Choose $0<\delta<r^2/4$ and $\varepsilon>0$ with $\delta+\varepsilon(L-b)<r^2/2$. Set
\[
 F=\max(\rho_a,\delta+\varepsilon(\log|P|-b)),\quad
 \rho_a=|x-a|^2/2,\quad u=F-\rho_a.
\]
The strict boundary inequality gives a tropical collar on which $u=0$, so extension by zero is continuous. Near a zero of $P$, $F=\rho_a$ on an ordinary neighbourhood. Elsewhere a smooth convex soft maximum of the two ordinary smooth psh weights approximates $F$ locally uniformly. Thus this function belongs even to the first approximation stage, without identifying that stage with all of $\mathscr P$. It has $u(p)=\delta>u(q)$.

The span $\mathcal D=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf R}\mathcal C$ is a vector lattice. Convexity writes its members as $A(p-q)$ with $p,q\in\mathcal C$. For a common $A>0$,
\[
 \max(A(p-q),A(r-s))=2A\max((p+s)/2,(r+q)/2)-2A(q+s)/2.
\]
Minima follow by negation. For any continuous $h$ and tolerance $\eta$, point separation and constants give $f_{xy}\in\mathcal D$ agreeing with $h$ at $x,y$. At fixed $x$, finitely many sets $\{f_{xy}>h-\eta\}$ cover $X$; their maximum $g_x$ is everywhere above $h-\eta$ and equals $h$ at $x$. Finitely many neighbourhoods on which $g_x<h+\eta$ cover $X$. Their minimum approximates $h$ uniformly within $\eta$. Hence $\mathcal D$ is dense in all of $C(X)$, including tests off the toric skeleton.

There is no global strictness assertion: on the residue bidisc $|z_i-1|<1$, $x_i=0$ and $\theta=0$. Curvature in moments $z_i-1$ cannot be bounded by a multiple of $\theta$ there. The later strictness argument uses other bounded potentials.

notes.detailedSummary: Checks corrected CLD source applications, reconstructs fixed-current Hilbert gradients and cutoff closure for the entire minimal continuous sheaf, and proves bounded products, variation, cocycle, concavity and comparison. Proves presentation independence, simplex polynomial energy and finite-dual integrability. Decreasing generated energy continuity requires an already generated limit; intrinsic recognition and net flattening are not inferred.

# All-stage bounded calculus and canonical generated energy

Use the actual surface and datum of n1. All assertions here concern the ordinary minimal continuous sheaf $\mathscr P$, not an assumed equality with a single smooth-approximation stage. The applied CLD v2 foundations, arXiv:1204.6277v2, are the following. Definition 8.1.7 and Lemma 8.1.8 define the minimal continuous sheaf and its transfinite uniform-closure stages. Lemma 8.5.1 gives $f_jT_j\to fT$ for locally uniformly convergent continuous coefficients and weakly convergent positive currents. Lemma 8.5.3 gives the smooth closed-factor differentiation rule. Lemma 8.5.5 gives positivity and closedness of $DD(fT)$ for continuous psh $f$ and positive closed $T$. Sections 8.7.1, Propositions 8.7.2 and 8.7.4 construct symmetric recursive products and their local uniform continuity. Sections 8.8.4--5 extend multilinearly to continuous dpsh functions and allow smooth $DD$-null potential changes. Proposition 7.2.8 identifies positive top currents with positive Radon measures, on locally differentially separated spaces; 7.2.11--12 provide smooth-factor measures and bounded continuous multiplication. Proposition 5.11.1 supplies compact-support Stokes/Green, with analytic boundary terms. Theorem 15.7.1 supplies the calibrated tropical calculus on separated pure-dimensional analytic spaces with their analytic boundary. The hypotheses hold by n1, and the boundary terms vanish on $X$.

All these applied statements and complete immediate proofs were read in the corrected literal-LF units. Smooth cutoffs, partitions, scalar density, calibrated integration and the underlying positivity calculus remain conventional published foundations. In surface degree $(1,1)$ the needed matrix cone is the positive semidefinite cone; only scalar and this degree's domination is used. General higher-degree strong-cone order-unit claims, continuous-multiplier closedness in 8.6.7, and equality of the first approximation stage with $\mathscr P$ are not premises.

For $u,v\in\mathcal C$ put $\theta_u=\theta+DD[u]$ and
\[
 B(u,v)=\theta\wedge\theta_v+DD(u\theta_v),\qquad MA(u)=B(u,u).
\]
Locally this is the recursive product of the actual continuous psh weights. It is symmetric, positive and local; smooth affine changes of local potentials glue it. Testing exact terms by $1$ gives $B(u,v)(X)=M=2$. Convex and maximum closure of $\mathcal C$ follow from convex combinations and soft maxima of smooth weights, then two successive minimal-sheaf arguments, each closed under uniform limits. Thus they hold at every stage.

Here is the additional Green proof, not a citation to the supplied ROOT chain. Fix a positive closed $(1,1)$ current $T$. Complete compact smooth $(1,0)$ forms modulo the null space of $\int a\wedge Jb\wedge T$. Symmetry and positivity give a Hilbert pairing and Cauchy--Schwarz. Use local seminorms $Q_{T,\chi}(f,g)=\int\chi\,d'f\wedge d''g\wedge T$ with nonnegative compact smooth cutoffs. Let $\mathscr H_T$ consist of continuous functions locally approximable uniformly by smooth functions with strongly convergent gradients in these seminorms. Finite smooth partitions patch the approximations: the gradients of $\sum\chi_i f_{i,k}$ are $\sum\chi_i d'f_{i,k}+\sum f_{i,k}d'\chi_i$. The two sums converge strongly by gradient convergence and uniform convergence, respectively. Products and cutoffs obey the same argument. Continuous bounded coefficients act in the completion, using scalar smooth approximation and the norm bound $\|fa\|\le\|f\|_\infty\|a\|$.

Gradients are unique. If smooth $f_k\to0$ uniformly and their gradients tend strongly to $a$, closedness gives
\[
 \int d'f_k\wedge Jb\wedge T=-\int f_k\,d'(Jb)\wedge T\longrightarrow0
\]
for every compact smooth $b$. The right pairing is a finite signed measure. Smooth forms are dense by the definition of the completion, so $a=0$. On local patches use tests supported in a larger patch and cutoffs to obtain the same conclusion on a smaller one.

If $f\in\mathscr H_T$ and $L_Tf=DD(fT)$ is signed Radon, then for compactly supported $g\in\mathscr H_T$, $\int gL_Tf=-Q_T(f,g)$. First prove this for smooth $g$ by smooth approximation of $f$ and current differentiation; then approximate $g$ uniformly and strongly, with a fixed compact cutoff. This implies the exact identity
\[
 Q_{T,\chi}(w,w)=\tfrac12\int w^2DD\chi\wedge T-\int\chi wL_Tw.
\]
Consider the sheaf of members of $\mathscr H_T$ with $L_Tf\ge0$. It contains smooth psh functions. For a uniformly convergent sequence $f_j$, choose nested cutoffs $\chi,\eta$ inside the neighbourhood of uniform convergence, with $\eta=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, and bound $|f_j|\le B$ on the whole support of $\eta$. For $\epsilon=\|f_j-f_k\|$ there,
\[
 0\le Q_{T,\chi}(f_j-f_k,f_j-f_k)
 \le\tfrac{\epsilon^2}{2}\|DD\chi\wedge T\|_{TV}
 +2B\epsilon\|\chi\|_\infty\|DD\eta\wedge T\|_{TV}.
\]
Indeed positivity bounds the mass of the two Laplacians by $2B\|\chi\|_\infty\|DD\eta\wedge T\|_{TV}$. Gradients are strongly Cauchy. On each smaller patch select smooth approximants with uniform and gradient errors below $1/j$ for a cutoff equal to one on that patch. This local selection proves uniform closure; it is not a flattening of unbounded presentations or a claim about a global uncountable family of seminorms. Positivity survives distributional limits. Minimality therefore puts every stage of $\mathscr P$ in this sheaf. Its vector span contains continuous dpsh functions. Finite patching on compact $X$ yields
\[
 \int fDD(gT)=\int gDD(fT)=-Q_T(f,g),\quad Q_T(f,f)\ge0.
\]

Define $E(0)=0$ and
\[
 E(u)=\tfrac13\int u\,[MA(0)+B(u,0)+MA(u)].
\]
For $u_t=(1-t)u+tv$, differentiation of this actual cubic and Green with $T=\theta,\theta_{u_t}$ give
\[
 E'(u_t)=\int(v-u)MA(u_t),\qquad E''(u_t)=-2Q_{\theta_{u_t}}(v-u,v-u)\le0.
\]
Consequently energy is monotone, concave, satisfies $E(u+c)=E(u)+Mc$, and obeys the tangent inequality. Integration of the quadratic Bernstein coefficients gives
\[
 E(u)-E(v)=\tfrac13\int(u-v)[MA(u)+B(u,v)+MA(v)].
\]
If $u\ge v$, each of the three nonnegative integrals is bounded by $3(E(u)-E(v))$. Bounded comparison follows from $w=\max(u,v-\epsilon)$ and locality: $MA(v)\{u<v-\epsilon\}\le MA(u)\{u\le v-\epsilon\}$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ gives $MA(v)\{u<v\}\le MA(u)\{u<v\}$, without omitting contact atoms at the intermediate stage.

Let $\mathcal G$ be the actual pointwise functions $u_j\downarrow u$, $u_j\in\mathcal C$, with $\inf E(u_j)>-\infty$. These are upper semicontinuous actual local CLD-generated psh potentials. Indeed the sheaf generated by smooth psh functions and decreasing limits is also closed under uniform limits with finite continuous limit: for uniform errors $\epsilon_j$, pass to a subsequence with $\epsilon_{j+1}<\epsilon_j/3$, then $f_j+2\epsilon_j$ decreases to the same limit. Zero errors are handled by a constant subsequence. Its continuous part therefore contains $\mathscr P$ by minimality, and $\rho+u_j\downarrow\rho+u$ belongs to that decreasing sheaf. This does not prove higher-dimensional classical curve-test recognition. The domain remains generated, not all intrinsic unbounded psh. Energy is canonical for EVERY such bounded continuous decreasing presentation. The decisive lemma is elementary: if $v_k\downarrow u$ are continuous and a continuous $a$ satisfies $u<a$ everywhere, the increasing open sets $\{v_k<a\}$ cover compact $X$, so one index works everywhere. Apply this with $a=u_j+\epsilon$, and reverse the roles of the presentations. Monotonicity and the constant rule give equality of both energy limits, including finiteness of the second. Order preservation follows by the same argument. An identically $-\infty$ limit would eventually lie below every constant $-A$, contradicting the energy bound.

Finite convex combinations are in $\mathcal G$ by bounded concavity. Energy on each finite simplex is a polynomial of degree at most three: bounded polynomial values converge at a finite unisolvent interpolation set inside the simplex, hence their coefficients converge. The resulting polynomial equals canonical energy at every simplex point. Such a set exists because no nonzero polynomial vanishes on an open simplex. Endpoints omit zero-weight functions, so there is no $0\cdot(-\infty)$ convention hidden in a sum.

One further continuity statement is crucial and has its exact restriction: if $u_k\in\mathcal G$ decrease to $u$ ALREADY IN $\mathcal G$, then $E(u_k)\downarrow E(u)$. For a continuous term $v_l$ presenting $u$, the open sets $\{u_k<v_l+\epsilon\}$ increase and cover $X$; here $u_k$ is upper semicontinuous. Apply order preservation, then let $l\to\infty$ and $\epsilon\downarrow0$. No automatic generation of the limit, net closure or global diagonal flattening follows.

For a positive finite Radon measure put $E^*(\mu)=\sup_{v\in\mathcal C}(E(v)-\int v\,d\mu)$. Constants force $\mu(X)=M$ when this is finite. Shift a presentation below zero, apply the bounded dual inequality and monotone convergence, and cancel the shift using mass $M$. This proves for every $u\in\mathcal G$ that $u\in L^1(\mu)$, its pole set is null, and
\[
 \int(-u)\,d\mu\le E^*(\mu)-E(u)\quad(u\le0),\qquad
 \int|u_j-u|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0.
\]
Bounded tangent gives $E^*(MA(v))=E(v)-\int vMA(v)$ for $v\in\mathcal C$.

notes.detailedSummary: Cubic boundary coefficients and dense continuous tests determine unique weak limits of genuine analytic bounded products for every presentation. Proves finite full dual, self moments, generated first variation, moving L1 estimates, indicator passage on nonopen comparison sets, mixed locality and contact-excluding exact clamps with explicit tails. These are generated-domain conclusions, not arbitrary intrinsic products or an arbitrary-measure existence theorem.

# Independent generated analytic operator, moments, and singular-set comparison

Use the carrier and dense test lattice of n1 and the independently proved bounded calculus and generated energy of n2. The domain is precisely $\mathcal G$: actual pointwise decreasing limits of bounded continuous members of the ALL-stage minimal continuous sheaf, with finite canonical energy. The conclusions below impose no invariance, radiality or support restriction on these potentials or measures. They do not recognize every intrinsic unbounded psh function or assert an arbitrary-measure equation theorem.

For EVERY presentation $u_j\downarrow u\in\mathcal G$ and fixed $v\in\mathcal C$, set $P_j(t)=E((1-t)u_j+tv)$ and $R_j(t)=E(tu_j)$. The degree-at-most-three coefficients converge by finite interpolation of the canonical energies. The exact bounded derivative identity is
\[
 \int vMA(u_j)=P'_j(0)+R'_j(1).
\]
It is valid at these boundary coefficients: the first derivative integrates $v-u_j$, the second integrates $u_j$. The limit therefore depends only on $u,v$. By linearity it exists on $\mathcal D=\operatorname{span}\mathcal C$. For any continuous $\phi$, choose $f\in\mathcal D$ with $\|\phi-f\|<\eta$. Positivity and mass $M$ give
\[
 \left|\int\phi(MA(u_j)-MA(u_k))\right|
 \le2M\eta+\left|\int f(MA(u_j)-MA(u_k))\right|.
\]
Thus ALL continuous-test integrals converge, independently of the presentation. Their limit is a positive functional of mass $M$. The compact-Hausdorff Riesz representation theorem (positive functionals on $C(X,\mathbf R)$ are uniquely finite regular Borel measures, with mass equal to the value at $1$) gives a unique positive Radon measure $MA(u)$ of raw mass two. These are weak limits of the genuine analytic bounded products, not inverse measures assigned by a dual recipe.

The bounded polarization identity
\[
 B(u_j,v_j)=2MA((u_j+v_j)/2)-\tfrac12(MA(u_j)+MA(v_j))
\]
then gives presentation-independent mixed limits $B(u,v)$, positive of mass $M$, since averages are generated and positivity passes from the actual bounded measures. If limiting weights are continuous on an ordinary open set, Dini's compact open-cover argument gives uniform convergence of the presentations on its compact subsets. CLD 8.7.2 identifies the limits there with the actual local continuous products. No such identification is claimed merely because an intrinsic weight is bounded but discontinuous.

Let $D_u=\lim_j\int u_jMA(u_j)=R'(1)$, a finite coefficient. Bounded tangent, followed by continuous-test weak convergence, gives
\[
 E(v)-\int vMA(u)\le E(u)-D_u\quad(v\in\mathcal C).
\]
Therefore $E^*(MA(u))<\infty$, so n2 makes EVERY generated potential integrable for $MA(u)$ and every generated pole set null. For $k\ge j$, the bounded cocycle gives
\[
 0\le\int(u_j-u_k)MA(u_k)\le3(E(u_j)-E(u_k)).
\]
Let $k\to\infty$, using the fixed continuous test $u_j$ and the known limit of the self moment, and then $j\to\infty$ using $L^1(MA(u))$ convergence. This proves $D_u=\int uMA(u)$ and
\[
 E^*(MA(u))=E(u)-\int uMA(u).
\]
The lower bound follows by testing the bounded $u_j$ in the dual definition. No unbounded moment was presumed in obtaining finite dual.

For $u,w\in\mathcal G$, the canonical polynomial $F(t,s)=E(tu+sw)$ on $t,s\ge0$, $t+s\le1$, satisfies
\[
 \partial_sF(1,0)=\int wMA(u).
\]
First prove this for bounded $w$ using bounded presentations of $u$ and coefficient convergence. For general $w$, let $w_l\in\mathcal C$ decrease to it. At every simplex point $tu+sw_l$ decreases to the ALREADY generated $tu+sw$. The generated decreasing-energy continuity of n2 and finite interpolation give coefficient convergence. Finite dual of $MA(u)$ gives $L^1$ convergence in the test slot. This proves the formula, including boundary derivatives, without flattening nested presentations. Zero-weight functions are omitted at endpoints.

Apply this moment formula to the polynomial in the segment point and a direction, or substitute that segment into the finite multivariate energy polynomial. Together with the self moment it yields the actual analytic first variation
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}E((1-t)u+tv)=\int(v-u)MA((1-t)u+tv).
\]
Every integral is finite. Values assigned to differences at common poles are irrelevant because these sets are null. Concavity passes from the bounded polynomials, giving the full generated tangent inequality.

If generated $u_j,v_j$ decrease to $u,v$ already in $\mathcal G$, they may be unbounded. Energies at every finite convex combination decrease to their canonical limit by n2; interpolation gives coefficient convergence. Bounded test moments give weak $MA$ convergence on $\mathcal D$, and density and common mass give it on all of $C(X)$. Polarization gives mixed convergence. The moment coefficient of $E(tu_j+sv_j)$ gives $\int u_jMA(v_j)\to\int uMA(v)$. With $u$ fixed, the same reasoning gives $\int uMA(v_j)\to\int uMA(v)$. Subtraction proves the important moving estimate
\[
 \int|u_j-u|MA(v_j)\longrightarrow0.
\]
All poles involved are null, so the absolute value equals $u_j-u$ almost everywhere. Mixed moments have the same limits by polarization; alternatively $0\le B(a,b)\le2MA((a+b)/2)$ gives integrability and null poles for mixed measures.

Passing bounded cocycles term by term using these moving moments proves the finite-integral identities
\[
 E(u)=\tfrac13\int u[MA(0)+B(u,0)+MA(u)],
\]
\[
 E(u)-E(v)=\tfrac13\int(u-v)[MA(u)+B(u,v)+MA(v)].
\]
No infinite integrals are subtracted. For $u\le0$, the first identity gives $-\int uMA(u)\le-3E(u)$ and hence $E^*(MA(u))\le-2E(u)$.

Here is a complete indicator argument for comparison, because weak convergence alone does not justify restriction to a discontinuous comparison set. Suppose $\mu_j\to\mu$ weakly have common positive mass and $a_j,b_j\in\mathcal C$ decrease to generated $a,b$. Suppose their moving $L^1(\mu_j)$ errors tend to zero, and for each fixed $l$, $\int(a_l-a)\,d\mu_j\to\int(a_l-a)\,d\mu$, and likewise for $b$. These hypotheses hold for $\mu_j=MA(c_j)$ when $c_j\downarrow c\in\mathcal G$, by the preceding moments; mixed measures also satisfy them. The fixed-$l$ limits tend to zero as $l\to\infty$.

For bounded Lipschitz $H$ and continuous $\phi$, first replace $a_j-b_j$ by $a-b$ using moving $L^1$; replace this by the continuous $a_l-b_l$ using the fixed-$l$ estimates; use weak convergence at fixed $l$; then let $l\to\infty$. This proves
\[
 \int\phi H(a_j-b_j)\,d\mu_j\longrightarrow\int\phi H(a-b)\,d\mu.
\]
At any level $\epsilon$ with $\mu\{a-b=\epsilon\}=0$, Lipschitz ramps sandwich the indicator of $\{a-b>\epsilon\}$; the limiting gap is bounded by $\|\phi\|\mu\{|a-b-\epsilon|\le\delta\}$ and tends to zero. Thus the same convergence holds with the strict-set indicator. Finite measures have at most countably many positive-mass levels.

Apply bounded comparison to $u_j,v_j-\epsilon$ and use this lemma separately with $MA(u_j)$ and $MA(v_j)$. At common atom-free positive levels it passes to $\{v-u>\epsilon\}$. Let such levels decrease to zero. The result is
\[
 MA(v)\{u<v\}\le MA(u)\{u<v\}\quad(u,v\in\mathcal G).
\]
For $w_j=\max(u_j,v_j)$, energy monotonicity makes the limit $w=\max(u,v)$ generated. Bounded locality on the ordinary open set $\{u_j-v_j>\epsilon\}$ and the same moving indicator lemma give
\[
 \mathbf1_{\{u>v\}}MA(\max(u,v))=\mathbf1_{\{u>v\}}MA(u).
\]
The limiting set need not be ordinary open. Equality follows first against continuous tests and then as restricted Radon measures: a finite Borel restriction of a finite regular measure on compact Hausdorff $X$ is regular, so Riesz uniqueness applies. Polarizing the identity for $(u+z)/2,(v+z)/2$ gives the mixed maximum locality identity with $B(\max(u,v),z)$ and $B(u,z)$. Poles of $z$ are null for all mixed measures by domination with the finite-dual $MA$ of an average.

For $u\le0$, $u^A=\max(u,-A)$ is generated, by the presentations $\max(u_j,-A)$ and energy monotonicity. Generated energy continuity and weak continuity apply as $A\to\infty$. Maximum locality gives the exact stronger formula
\[
 \mathbf1_{\{u>-A\}}MA(u^A)=\mathbf1_{\{u>-A\}}MA(u).
\]
These measures increase to $MA(u)$ and have limiting raw mass two. The ENTIRE contact set $\{u=-A\}$ is excluded. If $E(u)\ge-C$, finite dual of $MA(u^A)$ and n2 give $\int(-u)MA(u^A)\le3C$, and hence $MA(u^A)\{u\le-A\}\le3C/A$. For $u,v\le0$ the successive mixed locality identity is
\[
 \mathbf1_{\{u>-A,v>-B\}}B(u^A,v^B)
 =\mathbf1_{\{u>-A,v>-B\}}B(u,v).
\]
Its mass increases to two. With $E(u)\ge-C_u$, $E(v)\ge-C_v$, domination by $2MA((u^A+v^B)/2)$ and its dual bound $C_u+C_v$ give the discarded-mass estimate
\[
 \frac{2(2C_u+C_v)}A+\frac{2(C_u+2C_v)}B.
\]
These estimates include all contact atoms on the discarded side.

# A genuine all-test strictness estimate and its remaining separation gate

The following is a new advance using n1--n3. It does not assert that degeneracy of $\theta$ has disappeared. For bounded continuous dpsh $f,h$ and a positive closed current $T$, write $Q_T(f,h)=-\int fDD(hT)$, with its positive Hilbert interpretation from n2. Extend the notation to differences of positive closed currents by linearity.

For $a,b,w\in\mathcal C$, put $f=a-b$, $g=(a+b)/2$, $h=w-g$ and
\[
 I(a,b)=\int(a-b)[MA(b)-MA(a)].
\]
The bounded product expansion and Green give
\[
 I(a,b)=Q_{\theta_a}(f,f)+Q_{\theta_b}(f,f)\ge0.
\]
The exact transgression identity, including its SIGN, is
\[
 Q_{\theta_w}(f,f)-Q_{\theta_g}(f,f)
 =Q_{\theta_a}(f,h)-Q_{\theta_b}(f,h).
\]
Indeed the left side is $-\int fDDf\wedge DDh$ by the recursive dpsh product rule. Symmetry of the product makes this $-\int fDDh\wedge DDf=Q_{DDf}(f,h)$, which is the right side because $DDf=\theta_a-\theta_b$. No arbitrary continuous coefficient is asserted closed, and no global Hessian domination is used. Cauchy--Schwarz therefore gives
\[
 Q_{\theta_w}(f,f)\le\tfrac12 I(a,b)
 +\sqrt{I(a,b)\bigl(Q_{\theta_a}(h,h)+Q_{\theta_b}(h,h)\bigr)}.
\]

Here is an explicit uniform bound for the last factor. Normalize $a,b,w\le0$ by individual constants and assume their energies are at least $-C$, with $C\ge0$. Constants change neither the gradients nor $I$. By the finite-dual bound of n3, for $p,q$ among these potentials, $\int(-p)MA(q)\le3C$. Also $B(q,r)\le2MA((q+r)/2)$ and concavity bound its dual by $2C$, so $\int(-p)B(q,r)\le6C$. Since $|h|\le -w+(-a-b)/2$, it follows that
\[
 \int|h|MA(q)\le6C,\qquad\int|h|B(q,r)\le12C.
\]
Finally
\[
 Q_{\theta_a}(h,h)
 =-\int h\,[B(a,w)-(MA(a)+B(a,b))/2]\le21C,
\]
and the same bound holds with $b$. Thus the actual bounded all-direction estimate is
\[
 \boxed{Q_{\theta_w}(a-b,a-b)\le I(a,b)/2+\sqrt{42C\,I(a,b)}}.
\]
The numerical coefficient comes from $12C+3C+6C=21C$ in each current slot. This is a proved surface I-estimate for arbitrary bounded $\theta$-psh tests, not a proposed CLN bridge.

Now suppose $u,v\in\mathcal G$ and $MA(u)=MA(v)$. Take ANY bounded continuous decreasing presentations $u_j,v_j$, subtract fixed upper bounds from the whole presentations, and normalize a fixed $w\in\mathcal C$ below zero. Their energies have a common finite lower bound $-C$. All four terms of
\[
 I_j=\int u_jMA(v_j)-\int v_jMA(v_j)
 -\int u_jMA(u_j)+\int v_jMA(u_j)
\]
converge by the moving moments of n3. Equality of the limiting measures gives $I_j\to0$, and bounded positivity gives $I_j\ge0$. Consequently
\[
 Q_{\theta_w}(u_j-v_j,u_j-v_j)\longrightarrow0
\]
for EVERY fixed bounded test $w$. This conclusion is independent of both presentations. It is formulated as convergence of the actual bounded gradients; it does not define a gradient for an arbitrary discontinuous difference by fiat.

There is also a concrete local analytic consequence for bounded solutions. If $u,v\in\mathcal C$ have the same $MA$, the estimate gives $Q_{\theta_w}(u-v,u-v)=0$ for every $w\in\mathcal C$. Green and Cauchy--Schwarz with any compact smooth scalar test imply
\[
 DD((u-v)\theta_w)=0.
\]
This detects local divisors despite the vanishing of $\theta$ on residue bidiscs. To see it, let $P$ be a nonzero Laurent polynomial, and choose a lift chart $|x_i-a_i|<r$ centred at the tropical class of a point of its zero locus. Fix a smooth convex function $\chi$ on $\mathbf R$ with $\chi=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$, $0\le\chi'\le1$, and $\chi(t)=t-c$ for $t\ge1$. Set $\psi_N=\chi(\log|P|+N)$, extended by zero near its zeros. This is an ordinary smooth psh function: at a zero it is locally constant, and elsewhere it is a convex smooth function of a unit moment.

Choose $0<\delta<r^2/4$ and $\varepsilon_N>0$ so $\delta+\varepsilon_N\sup\psi_N<r^2/2$ on the closed chart. The global bounded potential
\[
 w_N=\max(\rho_a,\delta+\varepsilon_N\psi_N)-\rho_a,
\]
extended by zero, belongs to $\mathcal C$ by exactly the collar and soft-maximum proof of n1. On the FIXED smaller ordinary neighbourhood $\{\rho_a<\delta/2\}$, independent of $N$, its curvature is $\theta_{w_N}=\varepsilon_N DD\psi_N$. Hence $DD((u-v)DD\psi_N)=0$ there for every $N$.

The precise further source foundation is CLD v2 Theorem 16.7.3: on a boundaryless pure-dimensional analytic space, for a regular meromorphic function $P$, $DD[\log|P|]=\delta_{\operatorname{div}P}$. The complete statement and immediate proof, literal LF23468--23656, were read. Its proof uses compact tropical charts, the boundary product calibration of Theorem 14.7.2 and Stokes; those deeper inputs are conventional, not newly recursively audited. Our smooth torus chart and nonzero holomorphic $P$ satisfy regularity. The proof also explains why compact smooth top-test supports avoid the lower-dimensional zero locus. Thus $[\psi_N-N]\to[\log|P|-c]$ on those tests (indeed eventually exactly there), giving positive-current convergence $DD\psi_N\to\delta_{\operatorname{div}P}$. Applying the continuous-multiplier convergence of CLD 8.5.1 to the bounded continuous $u-v$, then differentiating, proves the new local identity
\[
 DD((u-v)\delta_{\operatorname{div}P})=0.
\]
It concerns actual analytic divisor currents, not an abstract tropical obstruction. It also shows exactly where bounded continuity was needed: multiplication through this divisor limit is not licensed for unbounded generated differences.

The remaining uniqueness gap is explicit. We have not proved that these vanishing gradient/current tests force the actual pointwise generated potentials to differ by a constant. In particular $Q_\theta=0$ alone cannot be used for that inference. Wanner's retained theorem, arXiv:1801.04713v3, assumes an algebraically closed complete nontrivially valued field and continuous functions on open subsets of smooth algebraic curves. Our $K=\mathbf C((s))$ is not algebraically closed. Its continuous curve recognition theorem cannot simply be cited here, and the generated unbounded divisor limit would require a separate restriction/integrability argument even after a justified field change. No higher-dimensional classical-psh recognition follows from one positive Hessian current. Artifact: n4.md, with the full proof in scoped-paper.tex and proof-companion.md. This strictness estimate and bounded divisor consequence are partial progress, not full uniqueness or P16.7 closure.
